newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemalan military police rebels to lay down guns.
newsitem.headline: Guatemalan military police rebels to lay down guns.

text.p: Hundreds of Guatemalan military police prepared to turn in their weapons on Sunday, ending a tense, five-day rebellion over terms of a peace treaty, a police spokesman said.

"Our personnel came to a peaceful understanding that the solution to this problem was to turn in their weapons. They will start coming out as civilians and we will restore services," Maj. Julio Cesar Linares of the military police told reporters.

Army troops and tanks had surrounded the barracks on Saturday night as hundreds of disgruntled military police holding the fortified compound demanded government negotiators promise them severance pay when they lose their jobs later this year.
So tense was the stand-off that troops and rebellious military police had a brief exchange of fire late on Saturday. No one was hurt.

The entire 4,000-member military police force will be disbanded this year as part of drastic army cuts the government promised when it signed peace accords on Dec. 29 with leftist rebels the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG).
The army has played a pivotal and at times brutal role in political life for much of Guatemala's recent history.
The war claimed an estimated 140,000 lives, many of them poor Indian civilians killed in army counterinsurgency campaigns.
The military police rebellion this week marked the first sign of military discontent over terms of the breakthrough peace accord.

Until Saturday, the government had downplayed the insubordination. A presidential spokesman had called it a "labor dispute." But on Sunday army spokesman Col. Otto Noack told Reuters the army had decided the uprising was a criminal act of rebellion.
Military police commander Leonel de Leon Guillen met on Sunday morning with Defence Minister Julio Balconi. Noack said the meeting was informational, not a negotiation.

According to Noack, Balconi told ex-president Ramiro de Leon Carpio, who also intervened to resolve the rebellion, that the government would not negotiate unless the military police turned in their weapons.
Approximately 400 military police, fewer than half of the number housed in the barracks, had refused to turn in their assault rifles and machine guns since Wednesday.
Hundreds of other military police continued to report to work at security jobs in banks, parks and government buildings during the rebellion, but many of them also supported the revolt.

Military police complained that the peace accords did not specify what, if any, compensation they would receive when they lose their jobs and said the URNG guerrillas had won a better deal than the military.
One general who was taken hostage at the police barracks on Saturday was released on Sunday morning, Noack said.
